meta.title: More Pitch, Less Admin: Automating Grassroots Football with TouchlineHQ
meta.desc: A project built out of a drive to do better in a space dominated by people and companies charging monthly fees for nothing

content:
---
id: touchlinehq
title: "More Pitch, Less Admin: Automating Grassroots Football with TouchlineHQ"
desc: A project built out of a drive to do better in a space dominated by people and companies charging monthly fees for nothing
created: 1778929589539
updated: 1778929589539
public: true
date: 2026-07-17
tags:
  - Ramblings
  - Tech
---
For years, my boys have played grassroots football. Like most parents looking to get their kids away from a screen, we latched onto any sport they showed an interest in. Football—and more recently, cricket—stuck.

Five years ago, I started coaching. It began more out of necessity than expertise. I’ve coached a gaggle of peers for each of my three boys, but eventually, the logistics became impossible. There’s only so much one person can do when they are spread thin across different age groups.

**The Volunteer Tax**

Through those years, I’ve seen the "behind-the-scenes" chaos of grassroots sports. It takes hundreds of hours of manual effort from a handful of unpaid volunteers just to ensure a town’s worth of kids get two hours of organised sport a week.

Our club isn't small—30+ kids at U6s, at least two teams per age group up to U14s, plus seniors, reserves, and an expanding girls' section. But as our town grows, the administrative burden grows with it. In my day job as a software engineer, I see this and think: _this doesn't scale._ We are relying on tens of volunteers performing hundreds of repetitive, manual tasks every single season.

**The "Software Engineer" Lightbulb**

I started looking at the existing market for club management software, and frankly, it’s broken. It’s either companies charging £30+ a month for a static site, or lone developers charging £200+ for outdated, rigid templates. Most importantly, none of these systems _truly_ integrate. You end up manually exporting/importing player data because the governing body (the FA) doesn't provide public APIs. You aren't buying automation; you’re buying another layer of manual admin.

I realised I didn't want to build "another product." I wanted to build a solution. My goal wasn't to monetise; it was to make things better. If I was going to do this, it had to be open source, and it had to be free.

**Enter TouchlineHQ**

Separately, I was fed up with the visibility of fixtures. Our league spreads games across multiple divisions, cup games, and friendlies, making it impossible to see the "big picture." The FA's "Full-Time" site is a nightmare for data consumption.

So, I built a scraper. By exploiting a records-per-page bug, I pulled every game across the entire regional league—historic and future—and converted them into manageable JSON and iCal files. I’ve been hosting these on GitHub, syncing my boys’ matches directly into our family Google Calendar. The time saved is massive, and the peace of mind is even better.

That experiment evolved into **[TouchlineHQ](https://touchlinehq.co.uk)**.

Whether you’re a club administrator tired of manual entry, or a parent who just wants a live, reliable calendar feed for your team, this is built for you. You can check out the current tools and setup a bespoke space for your club (FREE) at [clubs.touchlinehq.co.uk](https://clubs.touchlinehq.co.uk).

This is a work in progress, and since it’s open source, I’m looking for fellow devs, coaches, and tech-savvy parents to help build the tools that grassroots football actually needs.

_Let’s stop the manual grind and get back to the pitch._

**Solving the Secretary's Nightmare: Registration and Payments**

Once the fixture sync was running, I realised that the real "time-sink" for volunteers wasn't just scheduling—it was the administrative loop of registrations and sub-payments.

I’ve since expanded **[ClubsPlatform](https://clubs.touchlinehq.co.uk)** to handle the full lifecycle of club admin. You can now onboard teams and run the entire operation for free. The platform handles:

- **Frictionless Onboarding:** Stop wrestling with new software. You can import your entire player database using the exact same spreadsheet format you already export from the FA’s Full-Time system.
    
- **Automated Payment Tracking:** Integrated with GoCardless, the platform lets clubs set up subscription tiers that actually make sense and assign them at a team, player or registration level (e.g. "training only")
    
- **Live Reconciliation:** Stop chasing parents via WhatsApp or spreadsheet hell. You get a real-time, filtered dashboard showing exactly who has set up their subs and who is still outstanding—broken down by team, registration status, or payment standing.
    

It’s about giving volunteers back their weekends. Instead of spending Sunday night chasing unpaid subs or updating manual records, administrators get a clear view of their club’s health in one click.

**Privacy by Design: Why TouchlineHQ is GDPR-Friendly**

One of the biggest anxieties for any volunteer administrator is data protection. Handling sensitive documents, names, and birthdays for hundreds of children is a liability most volunteers are ill-equipped to manage.

I’ve built TouchlineHQ with a **"Privacy First"** architecture. The platform operates exclusively using the FA’s **FAN (FA Number)**. We do not store names, dates of birth, or any sensitive PII. By linking records to the FAN and storing only the necessary contact emails for parent/player communication, we significantly reduce the data footprint of your club.

You aren't just saving time; you're operating with a much safer, more compliant data model than most proprietary "walled-garden" systems that harvest and store your members' sensitive data.


Ultimately, TouchlineHQ is about more than just automating a few spreadsheets; it’s about reclaiming time for the people who actually make grassroots football happen. Whether you’re a developer who wants to contribute to a project that actually matters, or a club secretary tired of the current status quo, I’d love for you to get involved. This is open-source, community-owned, and built by someone who spends his Sunday (and soon to be Saturday) mornings on the pitch, not just behind a screen. Come see what we’re building at [TouchlineHQ](https://touchlinehq.co.uk) and let’s make the beautiful game a little bit easier for everyone.

content:
---
id: uoojlcm61q8yjpj82mfqfou
title: A quieter homepage and a simpler sandbox
desc: Small overdue tweaks to my homepage and sandbox, done with Grok one prompt at a time
public: true
date: 2026-10-20
tags:
  - Tech
  - Javascript
created: 1791385603476
updated: 1792511089269
---
This latest raft of changes hasn't been a big sweeping (potentially jarring) set of changes. It's been minor tweaks, improvements and back burner items I've been wanting to get to for years. A better loading experience and more data surfaced on the homepage plus a sandbox that's more scalable and polished.

A Grok promotion started this round of tidy ups. A prompt here and a quick preview deployment check there and it all stacks up. Because I'd had years of commits none of the new code feels like it's been crowbarred in by another dev. It all just feels like me.

Before, the homepage was arriving in pieces. The shell, then the photo, then the introduction. It now stays on the site-wide Pacman loader until the profile text, the photo and the latest post are ready. On a wide landscape screen the photo and its card sit on the left with the introduction and latest post stacked on the right. A phone or a vertical monitor still stacks them. Lovely. No conditional blocks in different places due to the device they're rendering on.

That card has had a few more passes since. Clicking the photo cycles through GitHub, Intervals, Goodreads and Last.fm and the card follows along. Each one leads with a featured item. My last PR, a little map of my last activity, the cover of the book I'm on or my top album's artwork. The detail lives behind a "This week's metrics" toggle on the same card.

Desktop had some awkward bits too. The bottom nav is now always in view across the whole site and the page scrolls inside it rather than the whole window. A lot of old 5rem margins are down to 1.5rem and the left column widens to 22rem on bigger screens. New blog posts also go live on their own now. A check every 15 minutes rebuilds the site if the CMS has changed and until then the 404 page pulls the post straight from the CMS.

The sandbox was a little grim. A sidebar I'd never given the time it needed (and had previously decommissioned on my blog page) was the main way of showing off little side projects. So the page grew a select and got bolstered with a handful of historic tinkerings. Some components got fixes along the way, like the Podcast Player flashing in before the URL was read. The select is now bound to `?component=` and the selected experiment isn't mounted until that slug is known.

I also added Factory Sim and megaChess. Both are imported from their own repositories (with their own test pages) rather than copied in. The browser half is Pyodide, the same trick I used at RPF to run Python in the page. `megaChess` in particular is an old one and I'm glad it's getting showcased. I've dipped in and out of it over the years. This pass finally puts the game itself on the site with cool pieces, layouts and editor mechanics. It looks decent and it's given me more ideas for the future.

All in all I'm glad I used Grok (any AI tool would've sufficed) to code like a developer, iteratively, rather than build out a brand new app or product. I'm glad it worked out too. It might've been less effective than me and needed more prompts than I'd have liked but it kept things moving when I couldn't.

name: blog.neural-foundry-year-one-reflections.md

meta.title: Neural Foundry: Year One Reflections
meta.desc: A year back hands-on at Neural Foundry and a look at what I've built and learned

content:
---
id: neural-foundry-year-one-reflections
title: "Neural Foundry: Year One Reflections"
desc: A year back hands-on at Neural Foundry and a look at what I've built and learned
public: true
date: 2026-05-29
tags:
  - Career
  - Tech
created: 1748534400000
updated: 1792506493723
---

It's been a year since I joined Neural Foundry and stepped out of management and back into a Senior Software Engineer role. That was a deliberate move. I wanted to go deep on the technical side again and properly get my hands dirty. I wanted to consolidate what I'd picked up in previous roles building web based systems and learn something new around MQTT and real-time device communication. Neural Foundry gave me exactly that.

Over the last 12 months I've become a core contributor to the Unified Robotics Platform (URP) and I've driven the Automation Engine forwards. This is my look back at what we built and what I've learned along the way.

A quick note on languages before anyone points it out. I came for the TypeScript. The dashboard and NX monorepo are very much TypeScript land but the Automation Engine is a Python/FastAPI microservice. So I've ended up spending a fair bit of time back in Python too.

## MQTT

Everything starts with how devices talk to the cloud. We went with MQTT because its lightweight pub/sub model suits constrained devices like Arduino and ESP32. On top of that we standardised topics and messages through the URP-Embedded framework so every device type speaks the same contract. Then came an end-to-end acknowledgement (ACK) system so we know a message actually got to a device even when the network is flaky. Then RPC over MQTT so the cloud can call a device capability and get a structured response back.

The protocol wasn't the hard bit. The shape of the messages was. They needed to be flexible enough for very different devices but predictable enough for the Automation Engine to parse. We went through several rounds of refactoring before we landed on something that worked.

## The Automation Engine

The Automation Engine orchestrates device commands. It runs a command execution pipeline with structured error handling and retry logic. It has ROS2 client packages that bridge our MQTT layer with ROS2's native communication for the robotics side. Those ROS2 packages get distributed through an Aptly repository which we automated. It all deploys with Docker and Kubernetes through multi-environment CI/CD workflows.

Building it meant thinking about failure all the time. Devices go offline. Networks drop. Commands time out. The pipeline has to cope with that and you need to be able to see what it's doing when it does.

## The Dashboard

On the frontend I built a React dashboard so users can actually see their devices and automations. It's a drag and drop widget library built on React Grid Layout so people can put together their own views. There are widgets for device status, workstation performance and inventory tracking. Layouts persist so they survive a page refresh and state lives in URL search params so you can share it across workspaces.

It was a good reminder that infrastructure is only as useful as the interface sitting on top of it.

## CI/CD

The least glamorous part and probably the most important. I redesigned the NX monorepo structure for faster builds and clearer dependency boundaries. Our GitHub Actions workflows got concurrency controls and affected detection so we stopped building things that hadn't changed. Versioning is now driven by the Git SHA so nobody has to bump versions by hand. The Python microservices got their own build pipelines separate from the Node.js ones. And there were plenty of Docker build fixes for both Node.js and Python across multiple architectures.

None of it is much to show off but it's what made everything else possible. Reliable CI/CD is the difference between shipping and stalling.

## Device Onboarding

Devices need a secure way to join the platform and tell us what they can do. Onboarding is a JWT based workflow. Once a device is in, telemetry-driven attribute detection maps its capabilities automatically. Device inventory and status update in real time and an event mapping system turns raw device events into something the rest of the platform understands.

## What I've Learned

**Design for failure first.** With embedded and robotics you can't assume the network is reliable or the device is online or that the command will succeed. Getting the ACK and retry systems in early saved us bolting resilience on later.

**Monorepo boundaries matter.** The NX restructure sped builds up but the bigger win was making dependencies explicit. When microservices and firmware deploy from the same repo you need to know what depends on what.

**The interface is the product.** The Automation Engine could be perfectly architected but if operators can't see what's happening it's not much use. The dashboard work has me treating observability as a feature from the start rather than an afterthought.

**Stepping back from management was the right call.** Being hands-on again, building event-driven systems with MQTT and shipping 100+ PRs has given me more technical depth than any amount of oversight would have. I haven't stopped leading though. Reviewing 425+ PRs across the URP monorepo has become my main way of mentoring, shaping the architecture and keeping code quality up. The difference is it's grounded in code I'm writing every day.

## By the Numbers

- 100+ merged PRs
- 425+ PRs reviewed across the URP monorepo
- Core contributor to 2 major platform systems
- 30+ PRs on the Automation Engine
- 25+ PRs on CI/CD and build infrastructure
- 20+ PRs on device communication and embedded systems
- 20+ PRs on the dashboard and user experience

## What's Next

The foundation is solid. Next up is scaling the device ecosystem, going deeper on ROS2 and making the Automation Engine smarter about orchestration. I'm properly excited about where it's heading.

name: blog.mr-manager.md

meta.title: Mr Manager
meta.desc: A year on from leaving my first Manager role I look back and reflect on why I left

content:
---
id: 64zb5jr9i387dhobfyz96kf
title: Mr Manager
desc: A year on from leaving my first Manager role I look back and reflect on why I left
created: 1775808181417
updated: 1775808181417
public: true
date: 2026-04-10
tags:
  - Career
  - Ramblings
---
I've been back as a Senior Engineer for almost a year now, moving on from a Software Engineering Manager role I never actually aimed for. I didn't think it was something I wanted - I just fell into it, gave it a good go and found there were parts I loved but also signs I'd avoid next time.

For most of my time as a manager I stayed hands-on. We were initially a small team responsible for some widely used apps, things broke and we were expected to fix them. That meant I needed to understand how things worked and get stuck in when they went wrong. My team size fluctuated between 2 and 8 engineers - bulked up with subcontractors towards the end - but over time I ended up managing more than 10 individuals as people and teams kept getting reshuffled.

Process became a bigger part of the job (that word still gives me chills now). Not what we were building, but how we were building it. I had to report on monthly hours spent on projects, give progress updates against plans, and that started creating friction with non-technical stakeholders and higher ups who didn't see eye to eye with how we worked. We were assessed more and more against our original quarterly plans rather than what we actually delivered. I felt like I was moving away from a well functioning agile team to waterfall delivery for what? Process.

The hardest part was when team members were going through a rough time, personally or professionally. It hurt especially when it was something I felt we could have solved as an organisation, or worse, when we were the cause of it. Tensions with non-technical team members grew too. At first it seemed like normal push and pull between differing viewpoints. Then things spiralled. Working relationships broke down, managers and HR got involved. I'd never experienced anything like it before, but I felt victimised, undermined and at the end of it all like a square peg in a round hole. 

Other parts of my life changed too. I stopped tinkering with tech outside of work. I stopped going above and beyond like I *normally* do when I'm enjoying **what I do**. I struggled sleeping properly for a while, and I started dreading Monday mornings. Running was the one thing that stayed - I ran more than ever in 2023, almost 1,100km, because I was enjoying everything. But halfway through 2024 my output dropped to 900km, my only sub-1,000km year. In 2025 I peaked and troughed, and I found myself getting increasingly emotional afterwards. Other things stopped too, like writing here.

Initially I enjoyed it, it was like being a senior with added responsibilities. Truth be told it was more of a lead dev role with small bits of admin and pastoral support. The team was clicking, working well and most importantly delivering. People left (mostly pay related but I think stagnation played a big part), reshuffles happened, projects got ambitious and processes and ways of working came into play, particularly around standardising them across teams. Now across the whole department we were only talking 20+ people in a handful of teams but it felt unfair our ways of working were getting changed when we were delivering. When we picked up an ambitious project **because** we could deliver it we had subcontractors added to the team to help. Ways of working came up again as they only worked one way and refused to change. It left the rest of my team with less autonomy and ownership whilst having to carefully juggle conversations at a factory floor level on a daily basis.

Looking back, I think what really changed wasn't the work itself but my relationship with it. When I was hands-on, I knew where I stood. Code shipped, problems got solved, feedback was immediate. As a manager, success became harder to measure. Was it the team delivering? Were people settled or settling or maybe too settled? Was it stakeholders being happy? All of those, maybe, but none of them felt like _mine_ in the same way code used to feel like mine. There were also decisions made for me that I then had to try and explain to the team. This probably sounds like standard middle management stuff but it was tough moving to this when things were working.

One of the main reasons I went for the role was because I enjoy enabling others to solve problems. I'd dabbled as a teacher and I felt those skills getting worked again. There's a pride that comes with fixing something yourself, rolling your sleeves up and getting stuck in **but** I found a real joy in enabling others to find their solutions to problems, particularly when I knew it had eaten away at them for a while. Over time I found myself getting less time to even do that though and effectively become a translator more than a practitioner, bridging gaps between what the business and product needs with what engineers can reasonably build. Some days that felt valuable. Other days it felt like I'd lost the thing I was actually good at.

The breaking point wasn't dramatic. There wasn't one single event or conversation that made me walk away. It was more like erosion - gradual, almost invisible until you suddenly notice the landscape has changed. I started dreading Mondays, then Sundays. Then Saturday evenings. I'd lie awake thinking about the week ahead, the conversations I needed to have, the difficult messages I needed to deliver or the interactions I'd walk into as soon as I signed in. I stopped tinkering with side projects, stopped reading technical content, stopped engaging with the skills I'd spent years building. Running became my escape, the one thing that was still purely mine, but even that started feeling like maintenance rather than joy. The biggest moment was when I realised I didn't really care at all. Sure there were people I cared about and I'd still fight tooth and nail for but towards the end we'd picked up a greenfield project I had very little drive and passion to actually deliver. It was a job.

When I eventually handed in my notice, people seemed surprised. To them, I'd been "doing well" - promotions, positive reviews, a team that shipped. What they couldn't see was the hollowing out. I couldn't articulate it well at the time either. It took months after leaving to properly understand what had happened, and even now I'm still unpicking it.

What I do know is this: I'm back to building things now. Not because managing was inherently wrong for me, but because in that environment I ended up in a version of it that disconnected me from the work I loved. The teams I managed were brilliant, genuinely brilliant, and some of the best people I've ever worked with. The failure was systemic as much as personal - structures that rewarded reporting over enabling, cultures that confused presence for productivity, and an organisation that needed managers to be something other than what I wanted to be.

If you're thinking about going into management, I'd say this: make sure it's for the right reasons and the right place for you. Not because it's the next step, not because someone suggested it, not because the money's better. Make sure it's because you genuinely want to help people build things, not because you want to build things yourself. They're related but not the same.

The exit interview cliche would be "I learned so much" and whilst it's true, I wish I'd learned it differently. I wish I'd protected the parts of the job that kept me connected to the craft earlier. I wish I'd pushed back harder on the process stuff that added no value and maybe at times just stopped pushing and pick my battles. I wish I'd been honest with myself sooner about what was happening.

But that's the thing about these roles - you don't know what you don't know until you're in it. And sometimes you need to live through it to understand it. Sometimes even then you only start to uncover it piece by piece a year later...

name: blog.learning-cpp-embedded.md

meta.title: Learning C++ on the Fly
meta.desc: Some reflections on picking up C++ for an embedded project while learning on the job, along with ways of working improvements that emerged from the experience.

content:
---
id: blog-2026-04-01-learning-cpp-embedded
title: Learning C++ on the Fly
desc: Some reflections on picking up C++ for an embedded project while learning on the job, along with ways of working improvements that emerged from the experience.
public: true
date: 2026-04-02
tags:
  - Ramblings
  - Learning
  - Embedded
created: 1743523200000
updated: 1743523200000
---

I've always believed the best learning happens when you're slightly out of your depth. Recently, I've jumped in the deep end by diving into C++ for our embedded client project - something I hadn't touched properly since university, and even then only briefly (and I hated it).

The merge of the initial framework and dummy project use case just landed, and while the code works, I definitely don't feel like an expert. But I do feel like I've picked up a few useful lessons along the way.

## The Technical Stuff

Getting back into C++ after years of Python and JavaScript was... humbling. The memory management aspect alone was a sharp reminder that "explicit is better than implicit" isn't just a pythonic idea - it's essential when you're dealing with actual memory allocation.

What surprised me most was how much the tooling matters. Setting up the build chain, getting the debugger working, understanding the compiler flags - all of this took time I hadn't considered. Years back I would've been stumped but thankful I had my pair programming partner Claude to lean on, a little more than normal and for general syntax and structure above all else. I mean header files!? Come on, I'm still not convinced.

## The Learning Approach

Perhaps the biggest takeaway isn't technical at all. Learning on the fly is uncomfortable, and that's okay. There's a temptation to hide the learning process, to only share the polished results. But asking questions, pair programming, and being honest about knowledge gaps has been more productive than trying to fake competence.

I've also learnt to trust the overlap. My years of Python and JavaScript haven't been wasted - patterns translate, concepts connect. It's less "learning from scratch" and more "adapting what I already know to a new context."

## What's Next

There's plenty more to figure out - performance optimisation, implementing testing strategies (in C++ I've still got no idea!), CI/CD for the embedded build. But the framework is in place, the dummy use case works, and we're iterating from there. The first commit was a big'un and took longer than I'm comfortable with but it's about knuckling down to normal iterative working patterns now.

If you're ever in a position where you need to pick up a new language or domain quickly, my only real advice is: start. Don't wait until you feel ready. You'll feel ready eventually, but you won't get there by waiting. I'm still not comfortable with C++ even after writing 4k lines of a greenfield project **but** I am happy with the project as a whole, the gaps that are left and how extendable it is.

name: blog.tools-shape-how-you-think.md

meta.title: Tools Shape How You Think
meta.desc: How the tools you choose quietly shape how you work, what you build, and what you even think is possible.

content:
---
id: blog-2026-04-01-tools-shape-how-you-think
title: Tools Shape How You Think
desc: How the tools you choose quietly shape how you work, what you build, and what you even think is possible.
public: true
date: 2026-04-01
tags:
  - Ramblings
  - Tech
created: 1743465600000
updated: 1743465600000
order: "11"
---

I've been thinking about this a lot recently. Not in a "what's the best IDE" way. More in a "the tools you reach for quietly shape the way you think" way.

## Notepad++ to VSCode

Years ago my team's IDE was Notepad++ and our version control was copying files into folders with a `v` prefix. That wasn't laziness. The tools available shaped what we thought was possible. Nobody talked about CI/CD because there was no CI/CD. Nobody talked about code review because there was no mechanism for it. The tools set the ceiling and we built to it.

When I swapped all of that for GitLab, Docker and Ubuntu the work didn't just get faster. The conversations changed. Suddenly we were talking about merge requests, branch protection and automated testing. Not because I mandated it but because the tools made those things obvious. The tooling didn't just support a new way of working, it suggested it.

Now I exclusively use VSCode. Sure I've dabbled with others (Cursor and Antigravity most recently) but I always go back. There's probably a bit of habit in there but VSCode is extensible, it changes based on what work you do and how you do it.

## Daily Notes

Same thing happened when I started journaling in Dendron last year. The template had sections for gratitude, affirmations, evening reflections. Sounded great in theory. In practice I half-arsed it most days and never once filled in the affirmations section. Habit is everything and I just wasn't in one with this yet.

So I adapted. Dropped the sections I never used. Moved yesterday's reflection to the morning instead of the evening because that's when I actually had headspace. Migrated to Obsidian when Dendron's remote vaults became a faff because I wanted to write from my phone as well as my laptop. The tool changed but the habit started to stick.

The interesting bit is that once the friction dropped, the thinking followed. I now exclusively use git-backed Obsidian vaults for a lot of my day. I've got my personal vault (this one, with aspects hooked up to my personal site for my blog and CV), my professional vault (with outcomes from conversations, hiring notes and potential useful tools notes) and even shared vaults around specific applications (including their infrastructure, aspects we want to improve but don't feel like a ticket yet and testing approaches - dev stuff).

## The Pattern

I keep seeing this play out. Python was the right tool for data-heavy nuclear simulations. JavaScript was the right tool for EdTech web-based code editors. Typescript is best for now where interfaces between services and devices need structure. None are better than the other. But each one shapes what you reach for, how you structure problems, what you think the solution looks like.

Give someone Notepad++ and they'll think in files. Give them Github and they'll think in branches. Give them a daily template and they'll start reflecting. Give them the wrong template and they'll stop.

The closest thing I have to a professional philosophy is this: if you give people the required tools and a degree of freedom they will reward you. I've seen it hold true everywhere since. But I'd add something to it now. The tools you choose don't just enable the work. They shape the thinking that leads to it. Choose carefully.

name: blog.covid-was-my-catalyst.md

meta.title: Covid Was My Catalyst
meta.desc: Looking back at how a pandemic, some scavenged hardware and a rogue off-grid network changed the entire trajectory of my career.

content:
---
id: blog-2026-03-31-covid-was-my-catalyst
title: Covid Was My Catalyst
desc: Looking back at how a pandemic, some scavenged hardware and a rogue off-grid network changed the entire trajectory of my career.
public: true
date: 2026-03-31
tags:
  - Career
  - DevOps
  - Ramblings
created: 1743379200000
updated: 1743379200000
order: "10"
---

It's been a long time since I've written one of these. Four years, a couple of jobs and a lot of life later I figured it was time to put something down. I've been reflecting recently on how I ended up where I am and no matter how I trace it back, it all leads to the same place. Covid.

## The Setup

Before the pandemic I was a physicist by education, engineer on paper, software developer in practice. I'd spent years pushing for modern tooling in an industry that valued planning documents and page counts over working software. I'd watched [TerraPower](https://www.terrapower.com/) do exactly what I'd been banging on about for years and achieve exactly what I thought it could do. There's nothing worse than that feeling.

We were running Python 2.4 on internet-isolated networks. Our IDE was Notepad++. Configuration control was `chmod r+x` and a prayer. Waterfall development cycles ran 8 months end-to-end. Releases (if you can call copying software into a folder with a `v` prefix that) were rare and painful. I knew there was a better way but had limited time and energy outside of work and the industry I was in wasn't interested in hearing it.

## The Catalyst

Then Covid hit and everyone went home.

I saw my chance. I got approvals from those directly above me then pulled development machines out of the office, wiped them, installed Ubuntu and built a small off-grid network from my home office. Docker, GitLab, Puppet, MySQL, all secured with SSL. A proper little DevOps stack cobbled together from hardware nobody was using. No approval process. No 6-month business case. Just a problem that needed solving and the freedom to solve it.

Within two months we'd gone from barely functioning to actually thriving. Configuration controlled code, merge requests for technical reviews, GitLab Issues replacing our Excel change tracker, automated documentation replacing waterfall reports. Seven engineers working remotely as if nothing had changed. It was basic by any software company's standards but for nuclear engineering it was genuinely revolutionary.

## The Reception

Here's the bit I still can't quite believe. I signed up for GitLab Community Edition and got an email calling for conference talks. I figured why not, fully expecting to be laughed out the room. A nuclear engineer talking about Docker and CI/CD? Come on.

[GitLab Commit 2020](https://gitlabcommitvirtual2020.sched.com/speaker/sra405) embraced me. DevOps Live followed. [Data Center Knowledge](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/devops/rolls-royce-embraces-devops-approach-drive-nuclear-power-project) wrote about it. The tech community didn't care that what we were doing was basic. They understood the drive for change better than any manager I'd talked to internally. They were using tools they knew were great and here was someone applying them in a context they didn't fully understand. That combination resonated.

The tools got my foot in the door but the overwhelmingly positive reception was because of the community and mindset DevOps instills. I love tech, but I love DevOps principles more. That hasn't changed.

## The Exit

Not long after, Central IT tried to take down my off-grid network. Method developments stalled. I found myself waking up at 2:30am, something I'd got used to during stressful periods but this time I knew the reason straight away. I wasn't meeting my potential.

I wrote in my resignation letter that I work best with flexibility. Give me room to breathe and I'll not only be more efficient in my work but I'll coach and mentor the people around me. The times I'd truly been given that freedom at Rolls-Royce were the times I considered the job my dream job. The solution was clear. Go to the industry that actually embraces agile working.

## The Trajectory

Since then it's been a proper ride. FinTech at [Koodoo](https://koodoo.io/) building loan origination platforms with GraphQL and Kubernetes. EdTech at the [Raspberry Pi Foundation](https://www.raspberrypi.org/) going from Senior Software Engineer to Engineering Manager, leading the team behind the [Code Editor](https://editor.raspberrypi.org/). Now IoT at Neutral Foundry working on a robotics and automations platform. Each jump built on the last and every single one traces back to that rogue Ubuntu server in my home office.

## What I Learned

I've been thinking about why it worked and I reckon it comes down to three things:

1. **Naivety is underrated.** I didn't know what I didn't know about DevOps. That meant I didn't overthink it. I just solved the problem with the tools available and it turned out to be enough.
2. **Constraints breed creativity.** No budget, limited resources, same output expectations. Those constraints forced a scrappy solution that actually worked better than anything we'd have got through official channels.
3. **If you give people the required tools and a degree of freedom they will reward you.** I believed this at Rolls-Royce and I proved it, and I've seen it hold true at every company since. It's become the closest thing I have to a professional philosophy.

Covid was awful. But for my career it was the catalyst I needed. I've been chasing fun challenges and new skills ever since.

content:
---
id: blog-2022-03-30-some-awesome-infrastructure
title: Some Awesome Infrastructure
desc: After some major upgrades to my site and some long overdue links with my self hosted setup I wanted to document some of my cool setup.
public: true

tags:
  - Ramblings

Hey so I've got every intention of this page being the single point of truth about my entire infrastructure setup. I'm a little worried this will

1. Miss some vital stuff
2. Get outdated quick

So instead of promising something I'll hate producing and updating I'll give a good overview here and make sure to include links to repositories and useful external sources.

Where to begin. I guess the simplest place is my domain [sradams.co.uk](https://github.com/adamsuk/sradams-co-uk-content).

* Domain bought from Google Domains
* DNS outsourced to CloudFlare
* Frontend Next.js site hosted via SaaS
* Backend subdomains a mixture of SaaS and self-hosted

### SaaS
I love nothing more than having a good excuse trial out a SaaS platform and integrate it into my ecosystem.
- Vercel - Frontend is dead simple, I love it. I've been using Netlify for a while now but like most things on my personal site I wanted to branch out, so my sites hosted on Vercel. It works a charm with Next.js (given it's made by the same company) and I've never had a problem or need to change it. Great SaaS!
- Heroku - My backend services are a little more complicated. For apps I've created like my [podcast API](https://github.com/adamsuk/podcast-express-api) I utilise Heroku, again AMAZING!

### Self Hosted
For established and prebuild containers I self host on a HP Microserver Gen8. I've been playing around with containers for close to a decade now and upgraded to a dedicated server setup 5 years ago (prior to that I repurposed old desktops). Before moving over to web dev as a job I used it for Plex on my local network, digitising my music and film catalogues. These days there's a lot more which you can find here. I've always maintained a boundary with my own services, preferring the GitHub integrations and DevOps that comes with it.

As I alluded to I host a fair amount [running locally](https://github.com/adamsuk/docker) and carefully open the door to my private network for specific services:
* [Plex](https://github.com/adamsuk/docker/blob/main/plexms/docker-compose.yml) - used less and less these days now streaming services are stepping up but during my wire cutting days I set it up and it came in useful during lockdown. No DNS records needed as it's all registered and routed through Plex with auth.
* [Nextcloud](https://github.com/adamsuk/docker/blob/main/nextcloud/docker-compose.yml) - self hosted cloud storage. Used more and more as a form of automated backups for things like photos on mobile devices but also extremely useful for sharing files. I used this for a long time on LAN but recently opened it up on a subdomain and love the flexibility.
* [Ubooquity](https://github.com/adamsuk/docker/blob/main/configs/docker-compose.yml) - an awesome comic and ebook service. Not utilised as much as I'd like but opened up via a subdomain on the off chance I want to read something whilst away.
* [Grav](https://github.com/adamsuk/docker/blob/main/grav/docker-compose.yml) - a recent addition but utilised and integrated into my blog on sradams.co.uk/blog. It's also available on a subdomain but I'm currently utilising it as a headless CMS and it's working a treat!
* [SWAG](https://github.com/adamsuk/docker/blob/main/swag/docker-compose.yml) - a prebuilt NGINX setup for enabling reverse proxies from docker networks. LOVE IT. Without it I'd need to rethink how I'd expose these services.

So I've recently fallen HARD for [Pico-8](https://www.lexaloffle.com/pico-8.php). If you've not heard of it it's an indie game platform designed to make developing a game simple. It's $15 and runs on a host of machines ... one of which being a Raspberry Pi!

With my new found love of small indie games, my passion for tech, a spare Raspberry Pi 4B lying around (I got when I joined the Raspberry Pi Foundation ... THANK YOU!) and an innovation day fast approaching I came up with a plan:
1. I want to build something both physical and virtual.
2. I want to utilise my new Pi.
3. I want my young boys to love my creation.
with step 3 being the real test and determines if I succeeded or not.

A few days before the innovation day I did some googling and found this beast, a [Game HAT for Raspberry Pi](https://www.waveshare.com/game-hat.htm).

Perfect. I'd heard of but never used RetroPie, now seemed like the perfect opportunity. There were tons of blogs, articles and comments about getting Pico-8 working on a RetroPie machine, my favourite being this [reddit post](https://www.reddit.com/r/RetroPie/comments/lurmu0/pico8_in_retropie_easy_uptodate_tutorial_with/), nice easy-to-follow steps with working links to code snippets, thanks rhinofinger!

That's the physical done - check. I'm also utilising my new Pi - check. Happy days.

Next onto Pico-8 game developing. I've tinkered with PyGame in the past and just want to make something simple and repetitive, my boys will love it. I'd previously made 80% of a game with my eldest which was a simple platformer with obstacles to avoid. Nothing too adventurous and plenty of room for expansion. So my plan is to:
- make a single character
- make a single background
- add platforms to the level
- add obstacles moving from one side to the other

This could be expanded in each area with:
- a character selection
- moving background and/or multiple locations
- randomise platform locations and/or increase/decrease number of platforms for different difficulties
- change obstacle size, location, speed

Lovely, looks like a decent plan!

### ... some time later ...

That was an AWESOME DAY!!! Pico-8 ... love it, game HAT ... love it, RetroPIE ... LOVE ... IT! Lua ... I might learn to love it.

I feel I was a little ambitious for the day. I've got my build, Pico-8 works with SPLORE (although I need to do a hard reboot to exit). My very own Pico-8 game is still very much based off tutorials. I've got a little man that can move left and right on something that looks like grass but other than that he can't do much.

Still my boys were pretty chuffed so I'm counting all of this as a massive win and something else to do between things.

name: blog.learning-ruby-and-ruby-on-rails.md

content:
---
id: blog-2022-01-19-learning-ruby-and-ruby-on-rails
title: Learning Ruby & Ruby on Rails
desc: With a change of jobs I've been studying up on my Ruby. Not only that but after using Nextjs, Expressjs and FastAPI I'm now delving into Rails!
public: true
date: 2022-01-19
tags:
  - Tech
  - Learning
  - Rails
created: 1642550400000
updated: 1642550400000
order: "6"
---

Firstly, it's been far too long! I need to write a completely separate post about the latter half of 2021, I won't delve into that here! This blog is all about my learnings with Ruby and Rails! Exciting stuff.

This is by no means a "how-to" guide on learning Ruby, instead it's more of a "how I learnt Ruby". It might be useful as a little "gotcha" guide but other than that this is a purely selfish post all for ME!

## Noticable Syntax Differences
Just a little interesting syntax stuff:
- Objects have an ~inspect~ method. It seems pretty comparable to `to_s` expect for `nil` where the conversion to a string is `""` but on inspect it's `"nil"` ... interesting
- Double arrows on an `Array` pushes a value to the last element, NICE!
- `:` 👀 ... ok this is different. We've got ourselves a new base type `Symbols` by the looks of things. Immutable strings for object keys, but a new base type so definitely not strings?!? I'm in!! Coming from a land of Javascript and Python the use of `:` keeps getting me!
- Array slicing is `array[_start_index, _length]` not start to end index! To do that you use `array[_start_index.._end_index`] for inclusive and `array[_start_index..._end_index]` to exclude `_end_index`.
- Array `pop` is as expected but need to remember `shift` and `unshift`!
- Hash looks like a python dictionary or javascript object to me with a [couple of differences](https://medium.com/@asiddiqui0692/are-hashes-in-ruby-the-same-as-objects-in-javascript-53bf7e4949c1)
- A non-existent Hash key returns `nil` similarly to `null` in Javascript. Use `hash.fetch(key)` to catch `KeyError` exceptions.
- [BLOCKS!](https://www.rubyguides.com/2016/02/ruby-procs-and-lambdas/) remind me of python lambdas
- Shovel (`<<`) over plus-equals (`+=`) ... this'll be a hard one to get out of ye ol' brain. (shovel modifies original variable)

There's always going to be little gotchas but what's really going to trip me up are the checks for empty variable types. I'm pretty much going to be reliant on trial/error and [cheatsheets](https://blog.arkency.com/2017/07/nil-empty-blank-ruby-rails-difference/) for a little while 😆

## Rails

On first glance it looks like a nice mixture of Django with a templating structure not too dissimliar from Jinja2. There's definitely a LOT but I understand the whole "rails" concept for this MVC approach.

One thing I need to get my head around are all the in-built methods, one being controller actions and their associated HTTP method and URL path. Luckily I found [this little cheatsheet](https://www.codecademy.com/article/standard-controller-actions).

I'm loving the boilerplate generators!! Similar to the inbuilt methods I just need to remember the important commands but 90% of the config is just given to you! Perfect. The true test will be updating an old rails app 👀

### Gotchas

- To `require` or not to `require` that is the question. By default rails requires a ton of stuff so classes and methods are pretty much available everywhere and anywhere ... except when they're not. One that keeps getting me is `helpers`.
- Rails-provided paths ... thanks rails for being ultra helpful but until I realise my paths have auto-generated variables I'm going to take a little longer setting up basic routing and redirects.

## Useful Links

[Koans](http://rubykoans.com/)

[Official Rails getting started guide](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/)

[Exceptions](https://www.honeybadger.io/blog/a-beginner-s-guide-to-exceptions-in-ruby/)

[Base Types](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/ruby-data-types/)

content:

id: blog-2021-06-04-devops-and-me
title: DevOps and Me
desc: Some ramblings on how DevOps has shaped my career to date. From life in a multinational corporate to finding happiness in tech, all thanks to the culture DevOps instills.
public: true
date: 2021-06-04
tags:
  - Ramblings
  - Career
  - DevOps
created: 1622764800000
updated: 1622764800000

---

I've been making random entries into this blog for a while now. That and conference season is coming back around I'm in full nostalgia mode. This post is personal and based on my professional experiences to date about how I am where I am.

For years I worked in the Nuclear industry with Rolls-Royce. I joined a department of ~50 people with extremely similar, vague job titles. I found code early with Matlab and C but feel in love with Python when I joined [SMRs](https://www.rolls-royce.com/innovation/small-modular-reactors.aspx#/). I dabbled, lead and pioneered some big changes in nuclear method developments, utilising aging codes such as [RELAP](https://relap53d.inl.gov/SitePages/Home.aspx) and [COBRA-TF](https://www.ne.ncsu.edu/rdfmg/cobra-tf/), all wrapped in Python. A couple of years later, during my second stint at SMRs, a Bill Gates led nuclear company called [TerraPower](https://www.terrapower.com/) were exponentially ramping up; they'd spent the last decade developing methods to exploit tech for design gains. I can tell you now there's nothing worse than someone doing what you always talked about and achieving exactly what you thought it could do.

I did what I could and as a result of Covid-19 pieced together hardware knocking around the office. I made a small off-grid network to run simulations remotely for a small team. I used Gitlab, Puppet, MySQL and Docker and hosted a bunch of servers from my home office. I spread the word through [GitLab Commit](https://gitlabcommitvirtual2020.sched.com/speaker/sra405) (because of an email I recieved calling for talks due to me signing up to the community version) and [DevOps Live](https://www.cloudexpoeurope.com/devops-live/virtual-2020) (due to the reception I had from Gitlab Commit), gaining traction in [internet blogs](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/devops/rolls-royce-embraces-devops-approach-drive-nuclear-power-project) with the Rolls-Royce name. What we were doing was basic, but due to the industry, impossible to get off the ground. As a result of the pandemic I had a chance and genuinely believed any tech-based company or conference would laugh us out the room. Instead they embraced us. We were using tools they knew were great for a purpose they didn't fully understand. They understood the drive for change better than any manager I talked to.

There's one reason my work and achievements over a short space of time reasonated in the tech industry more than my own ... DevOps. The tools I was using got my foot in the door, discussing interesting topics with people in all sorts of industries, but peoples overwhelmingly positive reception to it was because of the community and mindset DevOps insills.

I left the nuclear industry not long after. Central IT tried to take down my off-grid network and method developments stalled. I can't tell for certain what the feelings were towards my work but it was always seen as an experiment whilst I was there. It could've been something great, utilising tech to bring together dispersed development teams in different cities and companies.

I couldn't be happier with my decision. DevOps is now part of my day-to-day and I'm surrounded by like-minded people. Disciplines are (rightly) seperated, whilst DevOps blurs the boundaries and encourages openness. I love tech, but I love DevOps principles more.

See you at [DevOps Live 2021](https://www.cloudexpoeurope.com/devops-live/virtual-enterprise-evolution).

name: blog.what-im-loving-about-javascript.md

meta.title: What I'm Loving About JavaScript
meta.desc: With a move over to web development I've been studying up on my JavaScript. Having mostly developed in Python I've been pondering on the differences and loving all things JS right about now.

content:
---
id: blog-2021-07-21-what-im-loving-about-javascript
title: What I'm Loving About JavaScript
desc: With a move over to web development I've been studying up on my JavaScript. Having mostly developed in Python I've been pondering on the differences and loving all things JS right about now.
public: true
date: 2021-07-21
tags:
  - Javascript
  - Tech
  - Learning
  - Python
created: 1626825600000
updated: 1626825600000
order: "5"
---

Having spent years developing various bits of software in python I'm surprised how similar I'm finding JavaScript. For sure, I'm still digging around the basic syntax but this base knowledge has me eagering awaiting all the use cases I can apply this too!!

This post took me sometime to pull together. I wanted to do it all justice and be as accurate as possible. I'm learning everyday so this blog entry is already pretty outdated but I wanted to point out some key difference and explain why I'm loving JS so god darn much!

A lot of this post is comparisons against my base knowledge of Python.

## Nice in Comparison
### Falseness
One thing I loved in Python is readability, particularly in conditional logic. Something like
```
if this_condition and not this_other_condition
```
is awesome, reads like English and is easily understood when you know it's evaluating the true and falseness of variables `this_condition` and `this_other_condition`. This falls down in readability when you only care about falseness
```
if not this_condition
```
isn't really the same and ends up being more broken English. This is where JavaScript is awesome because rather than deciphering broken English all you need to understand is what `!` does to a conditional block;
```
if (!this_condition)
```
reads the same to me as pythons trueness evaluation but gets inverted in my head due to `!`. Readability maintained, check.

### Parentheses and Braces

I'm not going to lie and say I loved it straight away and I think a stint using C# helped but I'm now loving parentheses and braces! I used to love how python enforced a standard code structure by essentially using indentation to start and end various blocks but there's nothing more frustrating then finding out the reason your code didn't work correctly is because of a few missing spaces. Don't get me wrong, I'm sure it's just as irritating finding your coding isn't working due to parentheses BUT ... IDEs are pretty good at reminding you about brackets and tend to be pretty duff with indentation.

Come on though, even conditional blocks wrapped in parentheses just look and read so much better!

```
if (you_like_explicit_code_formatting) {
  console.log("you will LOVE JavaScript!")
}
```

I think it does come down to personal taste a little but I actually think it's one of those things coders love. Python is so accessible and a nice first language. At first there's so many other things to remember and the chances of being caught out by indentation is pretty low (you'll likely only be working at a couple of levels).

```
if you_dont_want_a_minimal_braces_syntax:
    print "Python 2 is for you"
```

Even Python 3 comes with more parentheses and braces so I must be on to something...

### No More KeyError or AttributeError

I've got to be honest, I'm loving the dot and bracket notation for accessing object properties in JavaScript. But what I'm loving even more is it's default behaviour `undefined`. No more `obj.get()` or wrapping `obj[key]` in ugly nested try/except statements for me!

### Async Out The Box!

I can't describe how much I'm loving this. For anyone that's dug around my Github I've written little snippets in python that aim to remove the [single-threaded nature](https://www.github.com/adamsuk/pyStuff/tree/main/multi_proc.py) but in all honesty that's not really comparing apples with apples. What javascript provides out the box is insane! I've got a lot of learning but I'm loving `promise`, `await` and `async`!

### Variable Declarations

So one of the things I equally love and hate about Python is how open variable assignment is. It's kind of insane actually. You can easily do something like this:
```
function print(msg):
    with open("print.txt", "w+") as f:
        f.write(msg)
```
and I can fundamentally change what an inbuilt function does!? This can cause MASSIVE issues in large projects with complex imports, something, somewhere could be changing something you intrinsically rely on.

With JS (ES6 in particular) introduces some pretty awesome variable definitions. Introducing `const`, `var` and `let`. Why am I loving these? Well ...

`const` - by far my favourite. I'm so used to anything being up for grabs and capable of being reassigned that being able to make any variable immutable is massive. Let me type that again for you Python devs ... I can make ANY variable IMMUTABLE! This includes functions ...

`var` - mutable variable definitions. I'm not going to lie it's a little annoying having to define what I'm used to as default in Python, but having the alternatives far outweigh this slight annoyance.

`let` - no more redeclared variables with this bad boy. My best use case for this is for unassigned scoped variables. And `let my_var` is much neater than `my_var = None`. So this makes up for the `var` definitions scattered about my code.


## What I Miss

### MATHS!

I never thought I'd say this because learning it was like hell (it's basically a language of its own) but I miss pandas. Most of my experience with Python was due to the need to deal with large amounts of data. From large amounts of pre-processing to manipulation of time series datasets... pandas made it easy! With JS trying to implement a simple equation is a nightmare.

But it's the right tool for what I'm doing now. It's just a pitfall for an otherwise awesome language.

## Summary

There's a lot of stuff here. Some of it opinion and personal preference so just try it for yourself.

I'm loving JS now but would I have used it previously in place of Python ... now. Python was the right tool for the job for a data-heavy solution. Would I trade JS for Python (utilising some web framework like Django) ... hell no!

JavaScript is cool as.

```
scott@rolls-royce:~$ ./introduction.sh
Hi, I'm Scott. I'm a Physicst by education, engineer on paper, and software 
developer in practice. My current position is Performance Methods Lead for the 
Rolls-Royce led UK SMR programme. I'd like to briefly outline the beginning of 
our DevOps journey.
scott@rolls-royce:~$ python at_the_beginning.py
So my first interactions with the UK SMR programme was 4 years ago as the new 
kid on the block in a small team task with developing a "cutting edge" analysis 
method to deliver results for a budding nuclear reactor design at a stage of 
design analysis had never fed into before. As the SMR programme was ramping up 
we remained in our current department at another location in Rolls-Royce. So we 
stood of the shoulders of our departments successes and aimed to push the 
boundaries. I don't want to down play our successes at this stage (because various 
papers and talks at nuclear conferences have been given on them) but if I shared 
our plans, developments and first release with anyone from a software background 
we'd have been laughed at, for quite some time.
scott@rolls-royce:~$ python at_the_beginning.py --summary
- siloed, internet isolated network on an aging system (by our own standards).
- minimal software development knowledge in the team (dabbled in C).
- predominantly python 2.4
- gedit (Linux side), jEdit (Windows side)
- waterfall development (8 months end-to-end)
- limited customer engagement (zero by the actual developers)
- codes needed to do our job (although old and worn, they worked) 
scott@rolls-royce:~$ python -m unittest tests/test_at_the_beginning.py
....F..F..FF
FAILED:
- customer requirements not met
- analysis method delivered late
- overspent
- zero configuration control (unless you claim chmod r+x ... which we did)
- god-dam carriage returns!
scott@rolls-royce:~$ ssh scott@smr
scott@smr:~$ nano migration_summary.txt
So at this stage we've released!  We've migrated (onto on-premise engineering
Windows-based PCs).  We utilised Anacoda! Moved to Python 2.7 (latest company
approved version). Adopted less configuration management (no approved tool
on Windows).  We operated a Operational Support Plan which aimed to "quickly"
update the method (with an update being no less than 400 engineering-hours).
We began to unittest our code with our common team IDE being Notepad++.  We
begin to track required changes to the method using Excel to sanction changes.
scott@smr:~$ source brexit
scott@smr:~$ echo PROGRAMME_STATUS
As a result of Brexit the team I'm part of deminished to zero over a period of ~2 years.
scott@smr:~$ shutdown



Last login: Weds 31 16:44:54 2018
scott@smr:~$ echo PROGRAMME_STATUS
After a substantial time away from the programme (working on other waterfall
projects) I returned as Performance Methods Lead.  I was the first of 5 team
members to be deployed onto the programme (mid-Fed 2020).
scott@smr:~$ nano covid
set REMOTE_WORKING = True
set REQUIRED_CAPABILITY = False
set WORK_DEMAND_PROFILE = 'LINEARLY INCREASING - OUT OF CONTROL'
scott@smr:~$ source covid
scott@smr:~$ shutdown



scott@home:~$ editor action_plan_a.docx
During the first few weeks I pulled together an action plan to get my teams
capability back up and running.  There was an intention to utilise modern
tools and alternative IT provisions to make ambitious code coupling intentions
possible.  Covid was my catylst. Plan:
1. Remove development IT provisions from the office
2. Repurpose this IT with Ubuntu to host an development/analysis network
3. Host a 'head node' to ensure all nodes have a centralised store
4. Use this 'head node' to host:
   - MySQL for sensitive data
   - Puppet to ensure common tools and required certificates on clients
   - GitLab to manage method developments and analysis inputs
5. All 'head node' servers are to be used in Docker to ease hosting each
   individual service.
scott@home:~$ cd initial_devops && docker-compose up -d
scott@home:~/initial_devops$ cat shared_vol/current_state
This initial server/client approach, utilising DevOps tools has worked
better than ever envisaged!  Our workload looked ever increasing before
hand as a result of being under-resourced but now every member of the team
works predominantly on their Ubuntu client node.  We regularly commit 
code and analysis input changes (along with using it to share other tools
too!).  We've now moved our change request register to GitLab Issues,
utilise the board for assigning development tasks.  2 months in we've:
- kept up with our work demand, whilst enabling remote working
- configuration controlled our method (including historic releases)
- altered the method to work on Ubuntu with MySQL
- added end-to-end encryption and restricted users to read_only data
- rebasedline our method following the programme hiatus
- utilised branches and merge requests to technically check the changes
- began to develop automated documentation (rather than the typical
  documents seen in waterfall approaches)
- expanded the network to 2 physicsts in the programme
- built another analysis code from source (doubling our code-base)
- kept up with analysis demands
- began to scope cross-method interactions
scott@home:~/initial_devops$ curl --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: WorthMoreThanMyPIN"
 "https://smr:1234/api/v4/issues?" | jq '.[0].title'
"Further develop our DevOps principles"
"Utilse CI/CD for all testing requirements"
"Use tools to build the method into a Docker image for use across platforms"
"Lock down branches to enforce mandated QA approahces"
"Futher automate our documentation"
"Utilise pipelines for testing purposes between branches"
"Push method into the cloud and scale to meet analysis requirements"
"Bring everyone else along with us"
scott@home:~$ echo HAPPINESS
Extremely, thanks to GitLab.
```

tags:

  - Todo

I want to get back into this keep pushing forward with front-end tech. Its been too long since I worked on a personal project.

What have I been up to... working mainly. But I wanted to document the cool tech I've been tinkering with.
- [Pulumi](https://www.pulumi.com/) - actual infrastructure as code! I wrote a PoC spinning up all sorts of GCP resources using only Javascript! It's early days but this has a ton of promise.
- Github Actions - I've been pretty knee deep in CI for well over a year now. Firstly I tinkered with Gitlab on a self-hosted instance spinning up dedicated runners, then I moved onto CircleCI. Github Actions is a complete breath of fresh air. The number of pre-existing integrations and support with GCP is insane! I coupled my Pulumi code with Github Actions spinning up resources in less than 30 lines of code!?
- Netlify - I've not played with this as much but it's on the horizon. This sites hosted by Vercel which is a similar offering but there's a heap of questions I need to answer before jumping into a no-code front-end platform in my day job.

That's all folks. Other than a smidge of Auth0, MongoDB and Checkly there's not much more to add.

Note to self: look into that Checkly terraform provider!

I wanted to give myself a little space to deploy some small, potentially bug filled nuggets... welcome MY SANDBOX!

My first addition is a little code I completed as part of an interview assessment. I applied for a Python Dev position and was handed a generic assessment with all sorts on it with the expectation of completing ~50%. My first submission was positively received but a few minor points and considerations were given. So with this I went all out and attempted a fairly hefty question about deploying a JavaScript based calculator or the big wide web. With zero JS or web experience I taught myself enough to give them something that'd host an instance on localhost. With this and more I heard absolutely nothing. Pan to less than 6 months later and I found my perfect job and learnt enough to put the same code (with a few minor tweaks to get it working on Next.js) on this site.

I couldn't be happier and I'm extremely glad I didn't give that particular company any more of my time :)

I'm sure I'll add all sorts in this sandbox. I've had a few in my time but normally these consist of random directories or a random bit of tech after I've install a new OS ... so they don't last long. This one's by far the most polished... mmmmm Next.js ....
